units.title: Monitoring with delayed labels and bounded service metrics
units.outcome: Monitor operations, data contracts and mature outcomes as distinct signals.
units.theory:
Monitoring observes a running system under incomplete information. Predictions and operational events can arrive immediately, while outcomes may arrive much later. A quality metric computed from whichever labels happen to be available can describe a selected population. Report label maturity and coverage before interpreting the number.

The first case has four predictions but only two mature outcomes at cutoff 5. It computes Brier loss on those two and reports the coverage explicitly. It does not replace the unknown outcomes with negatives. A real analysis should also investigate whether label delay depends on the outcome, entity or intervention.

The second case separates covariate shift from service latency and predictive quality. A large distributional difference is a signal to investigate, not proof that model accuracy changed. A p95 latency from five samples is an observed summary with limited precision, not a service-level guarantee. Monitoring should identify the population, time window, denominator and response for every signal.
units.syntax: Filter labels by their availability time, retain prediction identities and calculate coverage against the original prediction population. The example uses an actual two-sample KS statistic for a deliberately separated numeric fixture. Latency uses an explicit quantile method. The real service project keeps only a bounded number of process latency samples and labels that scope in its API.

worked.title: Evaluate only mature observations and retain coverage
worked.explanation: Predictions 1 and 3 have known outcomes by the cutoff. Their squared probability errors average 0.085. The two excluded records remain part of the coverage denominator rather than being discarded from the monitoring story.
worked.expected: Mature-label coverage is 0.5 and observed Brier loss is 0.085.

worked.title: Separate data and operational signals
worked.explanation: The second case shifts every input value by ten and computes a maximal KS statistic on the tiny fixture. It separately reports the chosen latency quantile. Neither signal is described as an observed change in target quality.
worked.expected: The shift statistic is 1.0; the observed higher-method p95 latency is 15 milliseconds.

exercises.title: Move the monitoring cutoff
exercises.task: Advance the cutoff and recompute maturity and coverage.
exercises.check: Newly available labels change the evaluated population.
exercises.hint: Keep the original prediction denominator.
exercises.answer: Record the cutoff and cohort identities. Comparing different maturity stages without adjustment can create a misleading trend.

exercises.title: Test outcome-dependent delay
exercises.task: Describe a process where positive outcomes arrive later.
exercises.check: Early observed quality can be biased.
exercises.hint: Availability may be informative.
exercises.answer: Investigate delay by outcome and cohort, and use an appropriate evaluation design. Do not assume missing-at-random labels without evidence.

exercises.title: Interpret drift
exercises.task: Explain what a KS alarm establishes.
exercises.check: It establishes a difference under the tested sample/comparison, not performance loss.
exercises.hint: Input and target behavior are different.
exercises.answer: Inspect data contracts and evaluate mature outcomes when available. A changed distribution can be harmless, harmful or even beneficial depending on the model and task.

exercises.title: Record metric scope
exercises.task: State whether a latency summary covers this process or a whole deployment.
exercises.check: The scope is explicit.
exercises.hint: A local counter is not a fleet-wide monitor.
exercises.answer: Aggregate with suitable identities and windows when designing a real service. Preserve reset/restart behavior in the interpretation.

exercises.title: Choose an action
exercises.task: Define what happens after a freshness or schema alarm.
exercises.check: The response is specific and bounded.
exercises.hint: An alarm without an action is incomplete operations.
exercises.answer: Use a reviewed reject, fallback, investigation or rollback policy. Avoid silently continuing with invalid inputs while reporting healthy service status.

exercises.title: Keep uncertainty visible
exercises.task: Describe the limitations of a quantile from five samples.
exercises.check: The estimate is visibly weak.
exercises.hint: A percentile label does not guarantee precision.
exercises.answer: Retain counts and distributional context, then collect representative observations for a meaningful service objective or comparison.

units.diagnosis: A quality improvement can come from changing label coverage. A drift signal can occur without observed performance loss. A latency counter can reset on restart. Inspect populations, windows and evidence types before triggering a broad model replacement.
units.transfer: Monitor operations, data contracts and mature outcomes as distinct signals. Keep their denominators and scopes explicit, and connect each to a reviewed response. The real local service demonstrates actual process metrics and stale-feature rejection without claiming production-scale observability.
units.lab: Monitor operations, data contracts and mature outcomes as distinct signals. Run both complete local examples, explain the changed assumption, and retain evidence for the six practice changes.

units.title: Accepted model pointers and rollback after failure
units.outcome: Activate and recover model state through explicit accepted versions.
units.theory:
A candidate model should not become active merely because a file was written. Activation needs accepted artifact identity, interface compatibility and a reviewed decision. Keeping the current pointer separate from candidate files lets a failed candidate leave the accepted model unchanged.

The first case validates a candidate hash before replacing the pointer. A deliberately incorrect expected hash causes rejection while the old pointer bytes remain exact. The second activates a new version and deliberately returns to the prior version. These are local file-state mechanisms, not a distributed transaction across every serving replica.

Atomic visibility and durable recovery are different claims. os.replace gives a useful local replacement boundary, but power-loss durability, remote filesystems, multiple writers and deployment-wide consistency need additional design and qualification. The real Docker project restricts activation to an owned control CLI, validates model structure before publication and keeps the predictor's state mount read-only.
units.syntax: Write a candidate under a versioned name, validate its identity, write a complete pending pointer and replace the current pointer atomically. The pointer records the resolved version and hash. A failed check occurs before the active pointer changes. Preserve accepted versions and define cleanup separately from activation.

worked.title: Reject a bad candidate before activation
worked.explanation: The first case activates v1, records the exact pointer bytes and attempts a v2 activation with a wrong hash. The old pointer must remain unchanged. This tests a specific failure boundary rather than only the successful path.
worked.expected: The failed candidate leaves the active v1 pointer byte-identical.

worked.title: Perform a deliberate rollback
worked.explanation: The second case activates v1, then v2, then v1 again. It checks the final version and absence of a pending pointer. A rollback is recorded as an explicit action, not hidden by deleting candidate evidence.
worked.expected: The accepted version returns to v1 with no pending pointer file.

exercises.title: Validate before switching
exercises.task: List the checks that must precede pointer replacement.
exercises.check: They include artifact identity and compatible structure.
exercises.hint: A valid filename is not enough.
exercises.answer: The service project also validates feature order, finite coefficients and positive scales. Broader model acceptance still needs its evaluation and operational evidence.

exercises.title: Retain failed evidence
exercises.task: Keep the rejected candidate and its diagnostic in an owned review area.
exercises.check: The failure remains explainable.
exercises.hint: Cleanup is a separate decision.
exercises.answer: Do not overwrite the previous accepted version or erase the failure merely to simplify directory contents. Apply an explicit retention policy later.

exercises.title: Reconcile an unknown response
exercises.task: Describe a timeout after activation may have completed.
exercises.check: The next action reads the pointer before retrying.
exercises.hint: Unknown outcome differs from confirmed rejection.
exercises.answer: Use the intended version/hash to reconcile actual state. Blindly repeating activation can create misleading audit history in a larger system.

exercises.title: Check bundle compatibility
exercises.task: Explain why rolling back only coefficients may be insufficient.
exercises.check: The feature/preprocessing contract must also match.
exercises.hint: Models consume versioned inputs.
exercises.answer: Restore a compatible model and feature transformation bundle. A file-level rollback can be technically successful while predictions are semantically wrong.

exercises.title: Separate local and distributed claims
exercises.task: State what os.replace does not establish.
exercises.check: It does not prove multi-replica consensus or power-loss durability.
exercises.hint: One filesystem operation has a limited scope.
exercises.answer: Use suitable synchronization, persistence and recovery mechanisms for the deployed environment, and test partial failures explicitly.

exercises.title: Exercise the real project
exercises.task: Use the local-system CLI to activate v2 and return to v1.
exercises.check: Actual HTTP predictions identify the selected version and restore exactly.
exercises.hint: The project is a separate longer-lived workflow.
exercises.answer: Retain its ownership marker and state. The checker verifies real HTTP, model integrity and replacement without retraining, while leaving external production claims out of scope.

units.diagnosis: If an invalid candidate becomes active, inspect validation order. If a rollback changes predictions unexpectedly, inspect feature/preprocessing compatibility and artifact identity. If a response is uncertain, reconcile the current version before repeating or cleaning operations.
units.transfer: Activate and recover model state through explicit accepted versions. Test failure before publication and exact rollback behavior, then distinguish local atomicity from the additional guarantees required by a deployed multi-process system.

units.title: Model cards, slice evidence and data minimization
units.outcome: Write a model card that is grounded in actual data, metrics and operational decisions.
units.theory:
A model card should make intended use, inputs, evidence, limitations and operational ownership inspectable. It is not a certificate produced by filling a template. A useful card must reflect actual evaluated populations, known failure modes and the decision process used to accept or reject a version.

The first case compares two synthetic slices with different sample sizes and true-positive rates. The counts remain visible, so a rate difference is not presented as a precise population conclusion. One parity metric does not establish fairness, and a model's appropriate use depends on context, harms, alternatives and an adequately designed evaluation.

The second case defines a small input allowlist and rejects an unnecessary email field. Data minimization reduces avoidable exposure and keeps the interface focused on its purpose. It does not establish legal compliance or prove that every allowed feature is appropriate. A real system needs separately qualified governance, access, retention and review processes.
units.syntax: Compute slice metrics from explicit confusion counts and retain their denominators. The card records purpose, permitted features, excluded fields, owner, limits and a rollback version. Compare incoming fields against the allowlist. Keep governance statements tied to actual evidence rather than treating an artifact's filename as approval.

worked.title: Inspect rate differences with counts
worked.explanation: Slice A has twenty observations and true-positive rate 0.8; slice B has ten and rate 0.4. The program reports both counts and rates. Interpretation still requires uncertainty, population and decision context beyond this tiny table.
worked.expected: The two TPRs are 0.8 and 0.4, with different sample sizes.

worked.title: Reject an unnecessary field
worked.explanation: The request includes email even though the declared model interface uses only usage, tickets and region. The program identifies that extra field and retains the card's stated limitations and rollback version.
worked.expected: Email is rejected by the allowlist and the card retains its synthetic-data limit.

exercises.title: Compute a denominator
exercises.task: Identify the denominator of true-positive rate for each slice.
exercises.check: It counts actual positives, not all rows.
exercises.hint: Metric definitions matter.
exercises.answer: Use tp+fn and retain the underlying counts. Accuracy uses a different denominator and can tell a different story.

exercises.title: Add uncertainty
exercises.task: Describe an appropriate uncertainty analysis for the slice comparison.
exercises.check: It acknowledges small samples and the sampling/design assumptions.
exercises.hint: A numerical difference is not a complete inference.
exercises.answer: Use a method appropriate to the cohort and dependence structure, with the original denominators. Avoid a universal fairness conclusion from one noisy metric.

exercises.title: Review the purpose
exercises.task: State which decision the model is intended to support.
exercises.check: The intended use is concrete.
exercises.hint: A broad label such as prediction is insufficient.
exercises.answer: Name the population, action, alternatives and limitations. Changes in intended use require fresh evaluation rather than reusing the same card automatically.

exercises.title: Minimize inputs
exercises.task: Remove a field with no justified role in the interface.
exercises.check: The accepted schema remains explicit.
exercises.hint: Availability does not justify collection.
exercises.answer: Review feature necessity and potential harms. Preserve the decision and test rejected fields, rather than accepting arbitrary payloads.

exercises.title: Record operational ownership
exercises.task: Identify who can accept a model and initiate rollback in a real setting.
exercises.check: The responsibility is acknowledged outside the fixture.
exercises.hint: An owner string is a declaration.
exercises.answer: Connect it to actual procedures, permissions and retained evidence. Do not describe this synthetic label as an implemented organizational process.

exercises.title: Bound the claim
exercises.task: Explain why this card is not a compliance certificate.
exercises.check: The answer separates documentation from external requirements and review.
exercises.hint: A template cannot establish every obligation.
exercises.answer: Use qualified governance processes and appropriate expertise for the real context. Keep this lesson's technical and statistical observations explicit.

units.diagnosis: A clean aggregate metric can hide a weak slice or a changed population. A long model card can still omit the actual decision and evidence. Avoid converting one rate check, a template or an allowlist into a claim of universal fairness, safety or compliance.
units.transfer: Write a model card that is grounded in actual data, metrics and operational decisions. Retain slice denominators, stated limitations and a minimal input contract, and identify which external governance claims require separate review.

units.title: A connected local ML product and real service lifecycle
units.outcome: Deliver a connected local ML product with actual tool execution and a reviewable acceptance decision.
units.theory:
The capstone connects actual components under one information and interface contract. Polars validates and prepares synthetic records. Feast stores feature snapshots and supplies the historical values used for training, then materializes the same feature contract into its SQLite online store. A fitted scikit-learn pipeline predicts from those retrieved fields, MLflow retains its metrics and model card, and a real ASGI request verifies the inference interface.

The training cutoff permits 77 mature labels, while forty later decisions form the declared evaluation cohort. The program independently checks that historical feature retrieval reproduces the expected source values and identifiers. Online inference also checks feature age before use. This makes the feature store an actual part of the computation rather than an unrelated demonstration next to the model.

The ordinary pad remains a bounded fresh-process investigation. The separate complete local-system project adds persistent owned state and a real loopback HTTP server. Its checker covers training, input errors, monitoring, activation/rollback, stale features, corrupted model bytes and predictor replacement without retraining. Those are actual local deployment observations, with external production populations, scale and organizational controls kept separate.
units.syntax: Run the complete reference in the data-engineering pad to inspect source-bound JSON reports. The first report records actual training/evaluation, feature-store and inference evidence; the second explains a deliberately blocked publication decision. For the longer-lived workflow, copy projects/local-system to an owned work directory and use its README/run.sh. Its state is separate from the classroom's saved code and notes.

worked.title: Connect the actual data and model boundaries
worked.explanation: The first case retrieves all 120 historical decisions through Feast, fits on 77 eligible rows, evaluates 40 later rows, materializes online features and submits an in-process HTTP request. MLflow readback checks the recorded metric, and the classroom report retains the contract and outcome.
worked.expected: All 120 requests reconcile, model input/output is valid, and the report identifies actual local tools and the no-external-deployment boundary.

worked.title: Block a candidate with inadequate evidence
worked.explanation: The second case has valid schema and artifact identity but only 0.1 mature-label coverage against a required 0.8. Publication is rejected and the accepted version remains v1. This demonstrates that structural success alone is insufficient.
worked.expected: The publication decision is false with an explicit coverage reason and retained accepted version.

exercises.title: Trace the training features
exercises.task: Identify where the actual training values came from.
exercises.check: They came through the registered Feast historical retrieval.
exercises.hint: Follow identifiers and time boundaries.
exercises.answer: Compare them with the independent prepared source and verify complete request coverage. A separate successful store demo would not prove this connection.

exercises.title: Review label maturity
exercises.task: Explain why only 77 rows enter fitting.
exercises.check: The training cutoff excludes labels not yet known.
exercises.hint: The retrospective table contains future outcomes.
exercises.answer: Preserve the cutoff and included identities. Do not select training rows merely because their prediction times are earlier.

exercises.title: Inspect the saved report
exercises.task: Read the feature contract, age, metric and source identity.
exercises.check: Each claim has a defined local scope.
exercises.hint: A report should be evidence, not a success slogan.
exercises.answer: Verify actual readback and distinguish package execution, numerical assertions, evaluation interpretation and deployment qualification.

exercises.title: Run the real local service
exercises.task: Use the copied project and its Docker-only instructions.
exercises.check: The loopback HTTP endpoint predicts from durable owned state.
exercises.hint: The pad itself does not keep a server alive.
exercises.answer: The project has explicit training, serving and control roles. Its checker proves declared local lifecycle behavior and cleans only its owned resources.

exercises.title: Exercise rollback and stale inputs
exercises.task: Activate the candidate, restorev 1 and test stale-feature rejection in the project.
exercises.check: Versioned predictions and diagnostics follow the contract.
exercises.hint: Do not change timestamps merely to hide stale data.
exercises.answer: Retain accepted artifacts, preserve true feature age and record the operational decision. Monitoring and publication are part of the product.

exercises.title: Write the final acceptance argument
exercises.task: State what supports release and what remains external.
exercises.check: It separates local evidence from broader deployment claims.
exercises.hint: Every assertion has a scope.
exercises.answer: Cite the data/interface contracts, actual tool results, diagnostics, persistent state and rollback checks. Identify additional scale, security, population and governance qualification required for a real use.

units.diagnosis: If any boundary fails, diagnose the earliest mismatched contract rather than relabeling the whole pipeline successful. Check request coverage, clocks, feature identity, preprocessing, model version, artifact bytes and actual service responses. Keep candidate output separate from accepted publication and preserve meaningful failure evidence.

Use the owned service project to test persistent HTTP operation and recovery, then specify the additional evidence needed before adapting the design to a real organization and population.
